title: Leo Burnett 1891–1971

paragraphs.text: Leo Burnett, founder of the multibillion-dollar advertising agency Leo Burnett Worldwide, had a career spanning nearly six decades, and an aptitude for inventing evocative, easily recognizable corporate identities which spawned many of the iconic images of US commerce. As copywriter Dalton O’Sullivan remembers from his time working under Burnett in the 1960s, ‘Unlike many agency heads, Leo wasn't puffed up with his own importance — no fancy suits, or expectancy he should be bowed down to. But heaven help you if you were lazy in your approach to dealing with one of his clients. However, if you had a well-thought-out idea, even if he didn't like it, he would listen — and even change his mind when you clicked off facts and figures to back it up. He lived and breathed advertising and he expected you to do the same.

Burnett's associates recall various techniques he used with his staff. In one, The Group Think, a team brainstormed a problem, a process whereby even the wildest idea would be considered. In another, The Creative Right Bower, Burnett would turn to his number one man to spark up dull campaigns and be a constant source of grist and material for the creative mill. Occasionally, in a move dubbed The Outside Expert, an outsider was brought in to evaluate a campaign. This did not sit very well with his existing staff, but in Burnett's defense, it must be said that after a consultant's visit, everyone tried a little harder. Then there was The Creative Review Committee, where campaigns were presented, reviewed by all present, then reworked. This was expensive and time-consuming, but Burnett felt it worthwhile if it helped them develop a better campaign.

Burnett’s advertising career began when he joined the Homer McGee agency in Indianapolis in 1919. Ad schemes in the early years of the century had been based primarily on a carefully worded argument extolling the purported qualities of the product being sold. Images were mere decoration for the argument. But by 1919 product claims were giving way to imaginary stories of consumers whose acquisitions were rewarded with popularity, success and romance. Burnett moved the image to center stage. Visual eloquence, he was convinced, was far more persuasive and poignant than labored narratives, verbose logic or empty promises.

Creativity, he advised, called for an intuitive ability to identify the ‘inherent drama’ within a product, through the use of down-to-earth, vernacular imagery. To explain this, Burnett repeatedly cited a 1945 campaign for the American Meat Institute. After careful consideration, he related, ‘We convinced ourselves that the image of meat should be a virile one, best expressed in red meat.’ At the time it was highly unusual, even distasteful, to portray uncooked meat in advertisements. Enthusiastically breaking the code, Burnett produced full-page ads depicting raw red meat against a bright-red background. ‘Red against red was a trick,’ he explained, ‘but it was a natural thing to do. It just intensified the red concept, the strength, and everything else we were trying to express.

One of the most enduring icons of advertising history was that devised by Burnett in a campaign for Marlboro cigarettes. Aiming at male audiences in the 1950s, a time when filter cigarettes such as Marlboro were seen as appealing mainly to women, Burnett introduced a tough and rugged cowboy on horseback, ‘the most masculine type of man’, he explained, to transform the image of the brand. Other abiding Burnett creations are the cartoon characters Tony the Tiger and the Green Giant, icons representing, respectively, breakfast cereal and canned peas for generations of consumers.

Burnett admitted he rarely wrote advertisements. ‘My greatest contributions have been in uncovering some basic concepts now and then, editing, and stimulating fine talent to do better than they ever thought they could. Perhaps the most significant factor contributing to Burnett’s success was this total dedication to the creative side of the business. As he noted, 'there's nothing with quite the marketing leverage of the brilliant copy idea.’ Like many other persuasion professionals of his generation, Burnett was obsessed with finding visual triggers that could effectively circumvent consumers’ critical thought. Though an advertising message might be rejected consciously, he maintained that it was accepted subliminally. Visual images evoked responses from the ‘basic emotions and primitive instincts’ of consumers, he believed. Burnett did not originate this idea. In his classic 1922 study Public Opinion, journalist Walter Lippmann maintained that pictures are the surest way of conveying a message: ‘A leader or an interest that can make itself master of current symbols is master of the current situation.’ Burnett was exactly that.

Evaluating Burnett's contribution now, in the 21st century, one is of two minds. Created during the springtime of US consumer culture, when sales pitches were infused with an unfettered sense of optimism, Tony the Tiger and the Green Giant come across today as old-fashioned, quaint throwbacks to the time when sugared breakfast cereal, canned peas and fat-marbled beef represented a healthy diet. Though Burnett's corporate talismans endure, they occupy a world where consumers are increasingly sceptical about the promises made about the products offered to them. On the other hand, the central principles that guided Burnett's practice remain prescient. In advertising copy, the conspicuous triumph of typography over text, of catchphrase over explanation, reflects Burnett's admonition that — to the public mind — visual form is more persuasive than carefully reasoned argument.

questions.prompt: According to Dalton O’Sullivan, what did Burnett require of his staff?

options.text: support for clients’ opinions
acceptance of his judgements
respect for his authority
dedication to the profession

questions.prompt: Which of Burnett’s managerial techniques motivated his staff to improve?

options.text: The Group Think
The Creative Right Bower
The Outside Expert
The Creative Review Committee

questions.prompt: What was the focus of advertising before Burnett joined the industry?

options.text: emotional appeals to the consumers most likely to buy the product
fantasy scenarios associated with the purchase of the product
graphic depictions suggesting qualities of the product
language describing positive features of the product

questions.prompt: Burnett’s campaign for the American Meat Institute was innovative because it

options.text: emphasised a feature of the product seldom seen in advertising.
used magazines then uncommon in the advertising industry.
promoted a product which was not widely advertised.
changed the public’s perception of the product.

questions.prompt: What does the passage say about the Marlboro campaign?

options.text: It created a symbol which has been imitated by many other advertisers.
It exploited a view of the product which was common during that era.
It targeted a group of consumers not previously attracted to the brand.
It employed an image not previously associated with cigarette advertising.

groups.sourceInstructions: Questions 32 – 35 Complete the summary using the list of words and phrases, A-I, below. Write the correct letter on your answer sheet.
content: Leo Burnett admitted to occasionally identifying fundamental {{32}} on which to base a campaign, but rarely composed advertisements or commercials himself. What he valued most in his field of work was {{33}} – the key to the success of his business, in his opinion. Burnett’s aim was to present striking visual stimuli that bypassed consumers’ {{34}}, and appealed to their {{35}} at a very basic level.
